slides.title: What are they and what is the point?

transcription.tex: A Cartesian equation relates \(x\) and \(y\), for example \(x^2-y^2=5\).\par Parametric equations express both coordinates using another variable, such as \(x=\sin t,\ y=t^2\).\par Each allowed value of \(t\) gives a point on the curve. Eliminating \(t\) does not always preserve the full domain or direction.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: How could we convert these parametric equations into a single Cartesian one?\[x=2t,\qquad y=t^2,\qquad -3<t<3.\]
What is the domain of the function?
The domain is the range of \(x=2t\). Applying the bounds on \(t\) gives \(-6<x<6\). Both endpoints are excluded.
The range is the range of \(y=t^2\). The minimum, 0, is attained at \(t=0\). As \(t\) approaches either endpoint, \(t^2\) approaches 9. Neither endpoint is included, so \(0\le y<9\).

transcription.tex: A curve has the parametric equations \(x=\ln(t+3),\ y=\dfrac1{t+5},\ t>-2\).\par (a) Find a Cartesian equation of the curve of the form \(y=f(x),\ x>k\), where \(k\) is a constant to be found.\par (b) Write down the range of \(f(x)\).

Exponentiate \(x=\ln(t+3)\).\[e^x=t+3,\qquad t=e^x-3.\]Substituting for \(t\) in \(y\) gives\[y=\frac1{(e^x-3)+5}=\frac1{e^x+2}.\]As \(t\) increases from \(-2\), \(t+3\) increases from 1, so \(x>\ln1=0\). Hence \(k=0\).

As \(t\) approaches \(-2\) from above, \(t+5\) approaches 3 from above and \(y\) approaches \(\tfrac13\) from below. As \(t\) increases without bound, \(y\) decreases towards 0.\par Neither limiting value is attained, so \(\boxed{0<y<\tfrac13}\).

transcription.tex: Use \(\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1\) to eliminate the parameter. Another useful identity is \(1+\tan^2t=\sec^2t\).
From \(\sin t=x-2\) and \(\cos t=y+3\),\[(x-2)^2+(y+3)^2=1.\]Every point on the circle of radius 1 centred at \((2,-3)\) occurs as \(t\) varies.

\(y=\sin(2t)=2\sin t\cos t\). Since \(-\pi/2\le t\le\pi/2\), \(\cos t\ge0\). Use \(\cos t=\sqrt{1-\sin^2t}\) to obtain\[y=2x\sqrt{1-x^2}.\]As \(t\) runs from \(-\pi/2\) to \(\pi/2\), \(\sin t\) increases from \(-1\) to 1. Thus \(-1\le x\le1\) and \(k=1\).
Here \(-\pi\le2t\le\pi\). The function \(\sin(2t)\) takes every value from \(-1\) to 1, so \(-1\le y\le1\).
